title: Household DNS filtering
body_md:
## The switchboard that can say no

Every visit to a site begins with a question you never hear. Your device asks a DNS resolver, a sort of switchboard, where the domain points. A filtering resolver can refuse to connect names it has classified as malware or phishing, and the page never gets the chance to load.

Providers differ in their lists, categories, test pages and privacy policies, so read a provider’s scope and data handling before you pick one. Cloudflare makes a handy example because its two services sit side by side. Its **plain** 1.1.1.1 is a general resolver and does no malware filtering. The filtering service, Families, has a malware-blocking mode at 1.1.1.2 and 1.0.0.2 and returns a blocking address for any domain it has classified.

Be just as clear about the limits. A filter can stop a known malicious domain before a page loads. It cannot judge a seller’s intentions, look inside an encrypted page, or reliably classify every new lookalike, and now and then it blocks a legitimate domain by mistake.

## Where the rule reaches, and where it stops

A phone leaves the home router’s rules behind the moment it steps out the door. Setting DNS on the router covers the devices that use its DNS settings while they are at home. Setting it on one device is narrower, and easier to test. A local blocker such as Pi-hole gives you more control, but it needs a machine someone keeps up to date, and its administrator may be able to read the query logs.

How far a rule reaches depends on where the setting lives. A DNS choice saved for one Wi-Fi network does not have to apply on cellular, while Android’s system-wide Private DNS can use the chosen resolver on both Wi-Fi and cellular. A browser’s secure DNS, a VPN or an app can also pick a resolver of its own. So “set on the router” does not mean “protects every device everywhere.” Encrypted DNS shields queries on their way to the chosen resolver; it does not filter or validate websites by itself. And if someone else runs the home network, agree on the policy, and on a way to reverse it, before you change shared settings.

## Test it, and keep a way back

Write down the original DNS setting before you change anything. Test with the resolver’s documented safe test page or domain, never by visiting a live malicious site, and check a device on home Wi-Fi and, separately, on cellular or another network if that matters to you. If a site you need fails, find out whether the resolver blocked it before you decide the site is dangerous, and confirm the service’s true address through an independent channel.

Cloudflare Families documents anonymous feedback for a mistaken classification, but its fixed modes offer no documented per-domain allow control and no household query log. A report promises no immediate unblock. If only one device’s Wi-Fi DNS was changed and access is urgent, deliberately restore its recorded trusted DNS for that one confirmed visit, then put Families back and retest. Until you do, lookups through that Wi-Fi setting get no Families filtering. If the resolver itself is unavailable, restore your recorded settings or use a trusted fallback.

DNS is one layer, sitting beneath browser warnings, updates, MFA and independent verification. A successful lookup is never a verdict on safety.

widget_config.goal: Choose one household DNS filter on purpose, test how far it reaches, and recover from a false block without dropping your other safe habits.
widget_config.today_action: On one device, find out which resolver is in use and what kind of setting it is. If you test a filter, use a safe test domain from the provider’s documentation, on Wi-Fi and again on cellular, and note whether the setting is Wi-Fi-only, system-wide Private DNS or overridden by the browser.
widget_config.scope: Explanation for home networks, checked 2026-10-20. The people and cases are invented. Cloudflare’s addresses illustrate one provider and are not a universal recommendation; device menus differ, and so do Wi-Fi-only and system-wide settings. Families has fixed modes and a feedback route for miscategorized domains, but no documented per-domain allow control. Categories can be wrong, and they lag behind new sites.

blocks.title: The fake that is too new to be listed
blocks.situation: A relative gets a parcel notice about a shop order, and it points to a newly created, parcel-themed domain. In this invented case the domain resolves, because the filter has not classified it yet. No real link is supplied.
blocks.analysis: A DNS answer here means one thing: this resolver did not block the lookup. The family opens the shop’s order history in its own saved app and enters no credentials at the address in the message.

blocks.title: The school portal that won’t load
blocks.situation: After Cloudflare Families malware filtering is switched on for the Wi-Fi profile of one test phone, a school portal the family knows well stops loading. The school, asked independently, confirms the portal’s official domain.
blocks.analysis: This may be a false positive. The family checks the phone’s DNS setting and sends Cloudflare’s anonymous miscategorization feedback. Families has no documented per-domain allow control or household query log, and feedback promises no instant access. For an urgent school task they may temporarily restore this phone’s recorded trusted DNS, visit the independently confirmed portal, then restore Families and retest. Until it is put back, that switch takes Families filtering away from lookups made through this phone’s Wi-Fi DNS setting.

blocks.title: A trial run for the household DNS
blocks.setup: Four invented checkpoints, each on a test device. Each step states the DNS setup in force; no shared router is changed and no live risky domain is opened.

steps.prompt: Checkpoint 1: a test device lets you set DNS for one Wi-Fi network. You want malware filtering, and the options in front of you are 1.1.1.1 and 1.1.1.2. Which do you choose?

choices.text: Enter 1.1.1.2, the documented Families malware-filtering resolver, in this test Wi-Fi profile.
choices.consequence: This Wi-Fi profile now uses a resolver with the category you asked for. No other network is configured by this step.
choices.explanation: Plain 1.1.1.1 is a different service from the Families filter.

choices.text: Use 1.1.1.1. It is the famous one, so it must block malware.
choices.consequence: You now believe in a filter that is not there.
choices.explanation: Check a resolver’s name and policy; do not guess them.

steps.prompt: Checkpoint 2: on a separate test device, Families is selected in settings. How do you confirm that filtering works without browsing a real scam?

choices.text: Hunt for a live malware link and open it, just to watch the block work.
choices.consequence: You expose the device for no reason.
choices.explanation: A lesson or a setup test never needs a live malicious destination.

choices.text: Use the provider’s documented safe test domain and write down the result.
choices.consequence: You test the setup without going near a malicious page.
choices.explanation: Providers publish test endpoints for exactly this purpose.

steps.prompt: Checkpoint 3: Families is set only for a test phone’s home Wi-Fi, not as system-wide Private DNS. The provider’s safe test is blocked on Wi-Fi but not on cellular. What does that show?

choices.text: Something must be wrong with the shared router.
choices.consequence: You may tear up a working setup for the wrong reason.
choices.explanation: No router setting changed here, and a phone can use different DNS on different kinds of network.

choices.text: The Wi-Fi-only DNS choice did not follow the phone onto cellular, so note that boundary down.
choices.consequence: You can now tell what this Wi-Fi profile covers from how the phone behaves on cellular.
choices.explanation: That result fits a per-Wi-Fi setting; Android’s system-wide Private DNS can apply on cellular too.

steps.prompt: Checkpoint 4: on another test phone, Families is configured only for its Wi-Fi profile, and a school portal the school has independently confirmed is blocked. What next?

choices.text: Check the phone’s DNS setting and report the possible false positive to Cloudflare. For urgent access, temporarily restore this phone’s recorded trusted DNS, then reinstate Families.
choices.consequence: Feedback goes in. A temporary switch on this one device may open the portal, but until it is restored Families does not filter lookups made through the phone’s Wi-Fi DNS setting, and the provider promises no instant unblock.
choices.explanation: What Families documents is feedback for a miscategorized site, not a per-domain allow rule. First confirm the portal through a channel the school is known to use.

choices.text: Switch off all protection and never revisit it.
choices.consequence: One block costs the phone its filtering indefinitely.
choices.explanation: A false block calls for a report and, at most, a deliberate change on one device that you then reverse. It does not call for dropping protection for good.

blocks.debrief: Play it again and keep four things apart: which resolver was chosen, how far the setting reaches (one Wi-Fi network or the whole phone), what the provider’s test said, and, separately, whether the site is trustworthy.

questions.prompt: In this lesson, what does the plain 1.1.1.1 address do?

choices.text: Resolves names, without the Families malware category.
choices.explanation: The filtering service has separate addresses.

choices.text: Promises that every phishing domain gets blocked.
choices.explanation: Neither plain DNS nor a filter can promise that.

questions.prompt: Your filtering resolver answers a lookup for a domain normally, with no block. What can you conclude?

choices.explanation: A lookup says nothing about who the seller is.

choices.text: Just that this resolver did not block this one lookup.
choices.explanation: A new or misclassified scam site can get through.

questions.prompt: Why might a browser ignore your router’s DNS filter?

choices.text: Its own secure-DNS setting may send queries to a different resolver.
choices.explanation: Some browser configurations take a path of their own.

choices.text: Router DNS always controls every browser query.
choices.explanation: That overlooks secure DNS and other overrides.

questions.prompt: A service you know is blocked. What is the best first step?

choices.text: Decide it is criminal and warn everyone you know.
Confirm its domain independently and look at why it was blocked.
choices.explanation: The block could be a true positive or a false one.
